name: Khecheopalri Lake
tagline: The sacred lake where birds are said to clear the fallen leaves
meta_description: Khecheopalri Lake (1,700 m), West Sikkim: the sacred wishing lake, its Lepcha and Buddhist stories, rules, the Maghe Purne festival, costs and how to reach.
summary: Khecheopalri is a sacred lake at about 1,700 m in a forest bowl, roughly 30 km from Pelling off the Yuksom road. Revered by Buddhists, Hindus and Lepcha, it is known as a wishing lake where, by local tradition, birds pick fallen leaves off the water. Allow 1–2 hours, or stay a night in the village.
intro: Khecheopalri Lake lies in a bowl of forested hills above Khecheopalri village, about 30 km from Pelling by a branch road off the Pelling–Yuksom route. A short paved path from the car park leads through prayer flags and a row of prayer wheels to a wooden jetty over the water. It is quiet even on busy days; signs ask visitors to keep silent.

The lake's name comes from Kha-Chot-Palri, which Wikipedia explains as the palace of the khecheo, the flying yoginis or dakinis, and it is described as the heaven of Guru Padmasambhava, who is said to have preached to sixty-four yoginis here. The Lepcha call it Sho Dzo Sho, 'Oh Lady, sit here', and Hindus also revere it. People from all these traditions come to make wishes.

The lake has been protected under a Government of Sikkim notification since 2001. Swimming, boating, fishing and feeding fish are not allowed. The best-known feature is the clean surface: by local tradition, birds pick up any leaf that falls on it. The village above has homestays and a small monastery, and old footpaths link it to Yuksom and Pelling.

story.title: Conch shells from the sky, and a lake that keeps itself clean
story.text: Several stories gather around Khecheopalri, and Wikipedia's article records more than one. In a Lepcha tradition, a couple saw conch shells falling from the sky, the ground trembled and spring water rose to form the lake, which became the home of Tshomen Gyalmo, a protective goddess of the Dharma blessed by Tara. Buddhists know the lake as a place of Guru Padmasambhava and the goddess Tara; some say its outline, seen from the hills above, resembles a footprint, variously described as Tara's, the Buddha's or Shiva's. The detail most visitors hear is about leaves. Although the lake is ringed by forest, by local tradition hardly a leaf stays on the surface, because birds pick them up as soon as they fall. Stand on the jetty in autumn and see for yourself. Whatever you make of it, the water is kept clean by rules too: since 2001 the lake has been protected by state notification.

little_known.fact: The lake has been a protected site under Government of Sikkim Notification 701/Home/2001, dated 20 September 2001, which is why boating, swimming and fishing are banned.
Some say the lake's outline seen from the surrounding hills resembles a footprint, described in different traditions as Tara's, the Buddha's or Shiva's.
Padmasambhava is said to have preached to sixty-four yoginis at the lake, which gives it the name 'heaven of Padmasambhava'.

facts: Sacred wishing lake, prayer wheels, leaf-free legend
Not needed; small entry or parking fee

highlights.title: The wooden jetty
highlights.text: A wooden walkway leads over the water past prayer wheels and flags, so visitors can reach the lake without trampling the shore. Walk out slowly and quietly; the stillness is the point, and in the early morning you may have it to yourself.

highlights.title: Watching for leaves
highlights.text: By local tradition, birds pick up fallen leaves from the surface. Stand on the jetty in autumn, when leaves drop, and look at how clear the water stays. Whatever the explanation, the lake is noticeably clean for a forest pool.

highlights.title: Khecheopalri village and gompa
highlights.text: Above the lake, Khecheopalri village has a small monastery and homestays. Staying overnight lets you walk down at dawn, before day visitors arrive from Pelling, and hear the forest wake up.

highlights.title: Old footpaths to Yuksom
highlights.text: Before roads, villagers walked between Khecheopalri, Yuksom and Pelling. With a local guide you can walk part of the old trail through forest and fields, a day hike of several hours that ends in Yuksom.

highlights.title: Maghe Purne full moon
highlights.text: On the Magh full moon, usually in January or February, pilgrims gather to pray and float butter lamps on bamboo rafts. Sources differ on the date, so confirm it locally before planning a festival visit.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps to Khecheopalri run from Gyalshing or Pelling only a few times a day, mostly in the afternoon going up and the morning coming down, indicatively ₹100–200 a seat. They suit travellers staying overnight in the village.

Most visitors come on a full-day tour from Pelling that includes the lake, the Kanchenjunga Falls and Yuksom, indicatively ₹3,500–5,000 per car. The lake alone costs about ₹2,000–2,800 return. Pelling to the lake is about 30 km, 1.5 hours.
Reach Pelling first, about 135–145 km and 5–6 hours via Melli, Jorethang, Legship and Gyalshing, and visit the lake the next day. Check current status before you travel in the monsoon.

costs: Full-day lake, falls and Yuksom tour
where_to_stay: Most travellers stay in Pelling, 1.5 hours away, at hotels such as Hotel Garuda (budget), Norbu Ghang Retreat and Spa (comfort) or The Elgin Mount Pandim (premium). For a quieter night, Khecheopalri village has simple family homestays, and Daragaon Village Retreat in Darap sits on the same road. Yuksom, about an hour on, has Hotel Tashigang, Yuksum Residency and village homestays.
tips: Keep silent near the water; signs ask visitors not to make noise.
Do not throw coins, food or offerings into the lake; it is a protected site.
Walk clockwise past the prayer wheels and remove shoes where signs ask.
Come early in the morning or late afternoon to avoid the midday tour cars.
Carry a light jacket; the forest bowl is cool and damp even in summer.

experiences.title: Dawn on the jetty at Khecheopalri
experiences.summary: Stay in Khecheopalri village and walk down to the lake at first light, when mist lifts off the water, birds call from the forest and the jetty is empty.
body: Day visitors from Pelling arrive from about 10 am. If you stay overnight in a Khecheopalri village homestay, you can walk down the path to the lake at dawn and have the jetty almost to yourself. In autumn and winter, mist often hangs over the water and lifts as the sun reaches the bowl.

Turn the prayer wheels as you walk in, then stand quietly at the end of the jetty. Local villagers sometimes come early to pray or light incense. Watch the surface: by local tradition, birds take away the leaves that fall on it.
Walk back up for breakfast with your host family, and ask them about the lake's stories. Accounts differ between families and communities, and hearing them first-hand is part of the experience.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight near Khecheopalri Lake?
faqs.a: Yes. Khecheopalri village, above the lake, has simple family homestays, indicatively ₹1,200–2,000 per person with dinner and breakfast. Rooms are basic, with hot water by bucket in some homes. We book families we know and arrange transport from Pelling.

faqs.q: Is Khecheopalri Lake open early in the morning?
faqs.a: The lake is an open sacred site, and villagers visit early to pray. Formal ticket counters may open later. Ask your homestay host about the current practice. Keep silent and respectful, especially at dawn when people come for prayer.

faqs.q: Will I see birds clearing leaves from the lake?
faqs.a: It depends on luck and season. The tradition is that birds pick leaves off the surface; what most visitors notice is how clean the water stays. Morning is when birds are most active. Bring binoculars and be patient.

experiences.title: Old village trail from Khecheopalri to Yuksom
experiences.summary: With a local guide, walk the old footpath that links Khecheopalri village and Yuksom through forest, fields and small settlements, the way people travelled before the roads.
body: Long before the Pelling–Yuksom road, villagers walked between Khecheopalri, Yuksom and Pelling on footpaths through forest and terraced fields. Parts of these trails are still used by locals and are walked by trekkers as a warm-up before the Goecha La trek.

The route drops and climbs through mixed forest and farmland, crossing streams and passing village houses, chortens and mani walls. It takes about 5–6 hours depending on pace and stops. Paths are not waymarked and branch often, so go with a guide from Khecheopalri or Yuksom.
Finish in Yuksom with time to see Kathok Lake and Norbugang before dark. Arrange for your car or luggage to meet you there. Avoid the monsoon, when trails are slippery and leeches abundant.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Khecheopalri to Yuksom?
faqs.a: About 5–6 hours on foot for most walkers, depending on the route and stops. There are big drops and climbs. Start early, carry water and snacks, and arrange for a car or your luggage to meet you in Yuksom.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Khecheopalri–Yuksom trail?
faqs.a: Yes, we strongly advise one. The paths are unmarked, branch often and pass through private farmland. A local guide costs indicatively ₹1,500–2,500 for the day and knows the safest route in current conditions, as well as the villages on the way.

faqs.q: When is the best time for the Khecheopalri–Yuksom walk?
faqs.a: October to November and March to April, when trails are dry and the weather mild. December to February is cold but possible. Avoid June to September: rain makes the paths slippery, streams rise and leeches are common.

experiences.title: Evening with a Khecheopalri homestay family
experiences.summary: Spend a night with a family in Khecheopalri village: home-cooked dinner, stories about the lake, and a morning walk down before the day visitors arrive.
body: Khecheopalri village sits above the lake, with a small monastery and scattered farmhouses among cardamom and maize. A handful of families host guests. Rooms are simple, with thick quilts in winter, and meals are cooked in the family kitchen.

Expect rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, local greens and pickles, with chicken or pork on many days; vegetarian meals are easy to arrange. Evenings are quiet: tea by the stove, conversation about farming and the lake, and an early night.
Families here come from different communities, and each has its own version of the lake's stories. Ask, listen, and do not expect a show. Pay in cash and leave rooms as you found them.

faqs.q: What are homestays in Khecheopalri like?
faqs.a: Simple and warm: a clean room in a family house, shared or attached bathroom, hot water sometimes by bucket, and home-cooked meals. Expect quiet evenings and early mornings. They suit travellers who value local contact over hotel comforts.

faqs.q: How much does a Khecheopalri homestay cost?
faqs.a: Indicatively ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night including dinner and breakfast. Rooms with attached bathrooms cost a little more. Pay in cash where possible, as card and UPI may not work reliably.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Khecheopalri?
faqs.a: Coverage is patchy. Some networks work in parts of the village, with weak data. Tell family members you may be offline for a night. Power cuts happen, so carry a torch and a charged power bank.

experiences.title: Prayer wheels and a quiet wish at the lake
experiences.summary: Walk the short path past the row of prayer wheels to the lake, make a silent wish as pilgrims do, and learn the rules that keep this sacred lake clean.
body: From the car park, a paved path of about 10 minutes leads through forest, prayer flags and a long row of prayer wheels to the lake. Turn each wheel clockwise with your right hand as you pass; each holds rolled prayers, and turning it is said to send them out.

At the jetty, pilgrims stand quietly and make a wish. Khecheopalri is known as a wish-fulfilling lake for Buddhists and Hindus alike. You do not need to follow any faith to stand respectfully at the water's edge.
Read the signboards on the way: the lake is protected, and visitors must not swim, fish, feed fish, throw coins or litter. Small shops near the car park sell tea, snacks and incense.

faqs.q: Why is Khecheopalri called a wishing lake?
faqs.a: Buddhists and Hindus believe wishes made respectfully at the lake are fulfilled, linked to its sacred associations with Guru Padmasambhava, the goddess Tara and, for some, Shiva. Lepcha tradition makes it the home of a protective goddess. Visitors of any faith are welcome.

faqs.q: Can I throw coins into Khecheopalri Lake?
faqs.a: No. The lake is protected by a state notification, and throwing coins, food or offerings into the water is not allowed. Use the offering places or donation boxes instead. Keeping the water clean is part of respecting the lake.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk to the lake from the car park?
faqs.a: About 10 minutes on a mostly level paved path with prayer wheels along the way. It is suitable for most children and older travellers. The jetty is wooden and can be slippery when wet.

faqs.q: How far is Khecheopalri Lake from Pelling?
faqs.a: About 30 km, roughly 1.5 hours by car via Darap and the branch road off the Pelling–Yuksom route. A car for the lake alone costs indicatively ₹2,000–2,800 return, or ₹3,500–5,000 for a full day including the Kanchenjunga Falls and Yuksom.

faqs.q: Why is Khecheopalri Lake famous?
faqs.a: It is a sacred lake for Buddhists, Hindus and Lepcha, known as a wish-fulfilling lake. By local tradition birds pick fallen leaves off its surface, so the water stays clean. It is also linked to Guru Padmasambhava and the goddess Tara.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Khecheopalri Lake?
faqs.a: There is usually a small entry or parking fee, indicatively ₹20–50. Fees change, so check current status before you travel. Carry small notes, as digital payment is not always available.

faqs.q: Can I do boating at Khecheopalri Lake?
faqs.a: No. Boating, swimming, fishing and feeding fish are all prohibited. The lake has been protected under a Government of Sikkim notification since 2001. Visitors reach the water by a wooden jetty and are asked to stay quiet.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Khecheopalri Lake?
faqs.a: October to May, in the morning or late afternoon. Autumn and winter are clear and quiet; spring brings flowers in the forest. The monsoon from June to September brings slides on the road and leeches on the path, though the forest is green.

faqs.q: Is Khecheopalri Lake worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, for its calm and its place in Sikkim's sacred landscape. It is not a big scenic lake like Tsomgo; it is a small, still pool in forest, and its appeal is quiet and stories. It fits easily into a Pelling–Yuksom day.

faqs.q: What is the legend of Khecheopalri Lake?
faqs.a: Wikipedia records a Lepcha tradition in which conch shells fell from the sky, the ground shook and spring water rose to form the lake, home of a protective goddess. Buddhists link it with Padmasambhava and Tara. By local tradition, birds remove leaves from its surface.

faqs.q: Can I combine Khecheopalri Lake with Yuksom?
faqs.a: Yes. The lake is on a branch road off the Pelling–Yuksom route, and most visitors see it on the same day as the Kanchenjunga Falls, Norbugang and Kathok Lake in Yuksom. For Dubdi Monastery too, stay a night in Yuksom.

faqs.q: Is there accommodation at Khecheopalri?
faqs.a: Yes, simple family homestays in Khecheopalri village above the lake, indicatively ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals. For more comfort, stay in Pelling, 1.5 hours away, or Yuksom, about an hour on.
